\\\"5988e3c4193ad460c13eb8faea45de9f7b7bfe0be976926db95a3178e087113c\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"excerpt\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"[EXCERPT extracted-character range 0:4500]\\\\n# K-TOOLS-004：框架 Profiler：算子归属、内存与图边界\\\\n\\\\n框架 profiler 把高层操作、主机提交、设备执行、shape、调用栈和内存活动连接起来。它提供的是特定版本、采集配置和窗口内的观测记录。解释性能时，需要先恢复执行实例及其依赖，再讨论耗时和资源；算子名称、时间接近或累计计数本身不足以建立因果归属。\\\\n\\\\n## 观测对象、身份与证据边界\\\\n\\\\n设采集窗口为 `W=[T0,T1)`，配置为 `C`，观测结果为 `O(W;C)`。`C` 包括模型与框架版本、执行模式、负载阶段、启用的活动、shape/stack/memory 选项及硬件条件。事件表示为 `x=(kind,domain,scope,id,[s,e),attrs)`：`domain` 指时钟或计数域；`scope` 保存采集运行、进程、设备、agent、队列等身份；`attrs` 保存 shape、字节、调用栈和关联字段。区间使用半开约定，结束于某时刻的对象与该时刻开始的对象不因此发生重叠。\\\\n\\\\n输入不仅包括事件，还包括字段语义、窗口覆盖情况、编译产物身份和时钟映射。输出包含实例关联、逻辑归属、区间统计、内存账本和未决记录。没有匹配的记录也是输出的一部分，不能因为它没有可用 correlation 就删除。\\\\n\\\\n| 证据 | 成立条件 | 能支持什么 | 仍不能推出什么 |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| 明确身份关联 | 字段语义已确认，关联键在对应作用域和代次内无歧义 | 某次提交与某些 dispatch 对应 | kernel 内每个融合子操作分别花了多少时间 |\\\\n| 范围、包含与顺序 | 范围身份或时钟可比较，依赖与队列顺序有依据 | 父范围、候选集合或先后约束 | 仅凭时间接近建立精确归属 |\\\\n| 聚合计数 | 采集对象、事件类型和运行范围明确 | 该范围的资源活动 | 无依据地拆成各 kernel 的贡献 |\\\\n| 缺失或截断 | 未启用、未覆盖、无权限或记录不完整 | 当前证据不足 | 零工作、零耗时或某个独有的 stall 原因 |\\\\n\\\\ncorrelation 连接身份，时钟校准连接时间坐标，两者不能互相替代。即使已经知道某个 API 提交了某个 kernel，也不能直接对两个未校准时钟的时间戳相减。完成时间映射后仍须保留误差界限；若间隔与误差同量级，应保留先后未知。\\\\n\\\\n作用域字段不是一套跨平台固定键。实际工具可能提供进程内 correlation、外部范围 ID、dispatch ID 或编译映射，API 记录未必直接携带设备队列。必须先解释字段如何连接；不能用缺失队列的默认值伪造身份。下文的完整键连接是一个字段齐全、提交键唯一的保守模型。\\\\n\\\\n## 算子、提交与 kernel 的多对多关系\\\\n\\\\n令 `L` 为逻辑算子实例集合，`A` 为提交实例集合，`K` 为设备 dispatch 集合。`P⊆L×A` 表示框架范围与提交的联系，`E⊆A×K` 表示提交与设备工作的联系，逻辑归属为 `R={(l,k) | 存在 a，(l,a)∈P 且 (a,k)∈E}`。关系通常不是一一函数。\\\\n\\\\n一个高层算子可能产生多个 kernel、复制或同步；多个算子可能融合进一个 kernel。一个算子也可能没有设备 dispatch：纯主机计算、惰性结果未求值、优化消除、工作被融合或采集缺失都可能产生这种现象。eager 与 compiled trace 的命名粒度变化不表示工作凭空消失，需要沿输入输出、生成计划和实际执行解释。\\\\n\\\\n同名重复调用必须保留调用实例。嵌套 host 范围中，父模块和叶算子都可能包含同一个提交：父范围的 inclusive 时间用于解释层级，不能与子范围相加成为独立资源成本。真正的融合共享归属也应与这种祖先包含关系区分。只有编译映射、明确标注或其他支持多算子关系的证据，才能把一个 kernel 记为多个逻辑操作共同实现。\\\\n\\\\nhost operator duration 与设备持续时间不同。主机范围可能包含参数准备、锁、图构造、入队和等待；设备区间描述所选 dispatch 的执行。异步 API 提前返回，只能证明提交边界发生变化，不能单独证明输出更早完成。设备 kernel 通常也不要求被短暂的入队 API 时间区间包含。\\\\n\\\\nshape 可以暴露历史重算、padding、KV 展开和非连续复制，但需要回到张量的轴、布局、存储身份、产生者与消费者。名为 concatenate 的操作可能真实复制，也可能先形成惰性描述或被后续融合；名称不能替代字节和执行证据。\\\\n\\\\n## 定义、求值、执行与消费的边界\\\\n\\\\n一个结果至少有五个不同边界：定义 `D` 创建操作或图描述；提交 `S` 请求执行；执行 `R` 表示实际设备工作；完成 `C` 表示相关依赖结束；消费 `U` 表示下游设备算子或主机取得结果。设备消费者可以通过依赖继续推进，主机读取则可能需要等待可访问的结果。\\\\n\\\\nMLX 固定惰性求值资料说明，操作先记录计算图，显式 eval 或访问结果才触发实际计算。打印、转换为数组、memoryview、保存和 scalar item 等访问可能触发求值；用标量数组决定控制流也会求值。未使用的输出可以不计算，但它的图构造仍有成本。过密求值支付多次固定开销，过大的未求值图又增加图级管理成本。这份资料的编译描述限于其固定文本，不能据此推断其他版本的全部编译能力。\\\\n\\\\n因此，计时图定义、计时提交和计时输出可消费回答不同问题。把读取移到后面，可能只是转移等待位置。合并求值可能减少提交和图处理次数，也可能延长中间状态生存期，改变峰值和并发供给，必须同时观察。\\\\n\\\\n编译、autotune、图捕获、可执行产物加载与图重放还会引入准备边界。首次调用和稳定调用应分别说明；shape 相同而 stride、dtype、guard 或 executable 不同，不能视为同一执行实例。设备指令 trace 依赖编译映射时，必须使用对应产物，不能拿另一版 NEFF 或生成计划解释当前时间线。\\\\n\\\\n## 采集窗口怎样推进\\\\n\\\\n采集从待裁决问题反推。先写竞争解释及不同预测，再选择能观察这些预测的活动。解释设备空洞需要主机准备、提交、同步和设备事件；解释临时复制需要 shape、布局和内存生命周期；片上资源解释才进一步需要对应计数器或指令 trace。\\\\n\\\\n以下状态是抽象采集协议，不是某一框架枚举或回调时机的逐字复制。实际接口可能把最后记录与保存合为一个动作，应保持其语义。\\\\n\\\\n```pseudocode\\\\n输入：负载；按步定义的采集计划；所需活动；作用域；窗口\\\\n输出：记录事件、覆盖区间、截断标记、采集配置与扰动说明\\\\n初始化：步号为0；记录集合为空；覆盖集合为空\\\\n对每个负载步：\\\\n    按计划确定本步为等待、预热或记录\\\\n    在执行本步工作前建立相应采集边界\\\\n    执行工作；保持请求、批次、线程和执行实例身份\\\\n    若为等待：将本步标为未观测\\\\n    若为预热：初始化采集路径；样本不进入正式统计\\\\n    若为记录：保存启用活动的事件和实际覆盖区间\\\\n    在步边界推进计划；若结束一段记录，刷新已有记录\\\\n结束时：\\\\n    记录保存是否成功，以及仍在途、截断或缺失的事件\\\\n    对每个持续事件与覆盖区间求交，保留原始身份和截断标记\\\\n    点事件按其自身时间戳规则处理，不冒充持续区间\\\\n    输出覆盖与未决状态；不把无记录区间填成零工作\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n记录窗口结束不等于异步工作完成。开始前已经提交的工作可能在窗口内执行；窗口内提交的工作也可能在结束后才执行。若问题涉及这些跨界工作，应扩大窗口，或保留连接到窗口外的身份及不完整标记。不能只按 API 是否落在窗口内决定所有设备工作是否属于该窗口。\\\\n\\\\n采集预热与模型预热也不同。前者初始化采集路径，后者可能初始化编译、算法选择、内存池和模型状态。丢弃采集预热样本不能证明模型已经稳定；短代表窗口仍须覆盖待解释的触发和完成转换。\\\\n\\\\n## 精确连接、候选连接与未决集合\\\\n\\\\n在字段齐全的模型中，定义提交键 `q=(run,pid,device,queue,correlation)`。假设一次采集运行内，此键唯一标识一个提交实例；一个提交可以对应多个 dispatch。若工具复用 correlation，必须增加能消除歧义的提交代次或其他明确身份，不能任意挑一个时间最近的 API。\\\\n\\\\n```pseudocode\\\\n输入：框架范围、提交记录A、dispatch记录K、字段语义及可选编译映射\\\\n输出：精确连接E、逻辑归属R、候选关系、未决集合U及原因\\\\n初始化：每个提交的dispatch列表为空；E为空；U为空\\\\n1. 规范化运行、进程、设备和队列身份；保留原字段和缺失标记\\\\n2. 检查实例ID唯一性；检查非空提交键是否存在复用或歧义\\\\n3. 对可精确解释且唯一的提交键建立索引\\\\n4. 逐个处理所有dispatch：\\\\n       若关联字段缺失：加入U，原因是缺少关联证据\\\\n       否则若完整作用域键没有对应提交：加入U，原因是未找到同域提交\\\\n       否则：连接到对应提交，保留一对多拆分关系\\\\n5. 用框架父范围或明确编译映射组合出逻辑归属；标注祖先包含与融合共享\\\\n6. 对未决记录，仅在字段、时钟和顺序允许时生成候选关系\\\\n       候选不删除未决状态，也不提升为精确连接\\\\n7. 验证：精确匹配过的dispatch与U不相交，两者并集恰好覆盖全部K\\\\n8. 输出关联、候选、未决原因、截断及采集条件\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n关键不变量是完整分区。令 `M={k | 存在a使(a,k)∈E}`，则 `M∩U=∅` 且 `M∪U=K`。未决不只包括 correlation 为空的记录，也包括 correlation 存在但没有同域提交的记录。一个记录不能因被拒绝精确关联而从账本消失。缺失标记也不能用一般的真假判断代替：若字段契约允许数值0或空字符串作为有效 ID，它们仍是有效键。\\\\n\\\\n设 L1 在进程1、设备0、队列0提交 correlation c1，产生 K1、K5；另有 K7 的 correlation 也是 c1，但队列为1，且没有该队列的匹配提交；K4 则缺少 correlation。此模型下，L1 精确关联 K1、K5，未决集合应包含 K7 与 K4。只保留 K4 会丢失 K7；只按 c1 连接则会把 K7 错接给 L1。若之后取得明确的跨队列提交映射，可以修订 K7 的证据状态，但不能靠放宽键完成修复。\\\\n\\\\n主机父范围的包含关系可以恢复调用层级；设备区间相对 API 的包含与时间邻近通常只能提供弱候选。异步排队、多个线程和多队列使最近邻规则尤其容易出错。聚合计数应连接到其真实采集范围；跨多个 dispatch 的计数器没有额外拆分依据时仍是聚合量。\\\\n\\\\n## 重叠时间与共享归属怎样列账\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 8000:12000]\\\\nystems的API、stream、copy和主机范围 | Nsight Compute的kernel计数器 | 沿明确范围和correlation关联具体实例；系统时间线与计数器采集分别解释 |\\\\n| ROCm | rocprofv3的HIP/HSA、dispatch、复制、分配与迁移等记录 | 设备计数、dispatch计数和其他受支持能力 | 保留进程、agent、queue与dispatch身份；能力与指标组合须核实目标设备 |\\\\n| Metal/MLX | 求值边界、对象标签与capture窗口 | 固定版本支持的GPU capture及Xcode操作依赖 | 捕获实际求值产生的工作；该来源没有证明完整Instruments或所有计数器覆盖 |\\\\n| Trainium | Neuron Explorer中的runtime、框架函数和HBM分配 | NeuronCore指令起止、DMA与计算引擎 | NTFF事件与对应编译NEFF后处理关联，系统长调用不能直接证明片上瓶颈 |\\\\n| CPU | 框架范围与进程、线程、CPU集合或cgroup | perf可用的cycles、instructions、cache等事件 | 保留计数对象、事件组、运行范围和聚合方式；不能把CPU信号解释成GPU stall |\\\\n\\\\nROCprofiler固定README区分API trace与设备、dispatch计数等能力；gfx11/gfx12的counter collection有稳定电源状态条件。列出能力不表示当前设备、权限与指标组合已经满足；多次采集时每次身份、条件和额外成本分别保留。\\\\n\\\\nMLX固定Metal文档说明调试选项可以记录Metal编译源码并标记对象，capture需要允许捕获的环境，可在Xcode打开和重放trace、查看依赖。构图发生在窗口内但实际求值发生在窗口外时，不能以capture缺失推断无设备工作。\\\\n\\\\nNeuron Explorer系统视图显示runtime和框架函数，并可连接硬件事件与HBM分配；设备trace用起止事件和编译NEFF形成详细报告。NKI架构资料进一步区分HBM、SBUF、PSUM、DMA和计算引擎。因此，解释片上数据供给应落到对应搬运和计算依赖，不能由主机runtime时长直接推断Tensor Engine饱和。\\\\n\\\\nCPU的 `IPC=instructions/cycles` 需要分子分母的计数范围可比。perf固定手册说明，事件是否共同调度、multiplexing和聚合方式影响指标解释；低IPC仍允许访存、依赖、分支或调度等竞争解释。跨厂商同名utilization可能使用不同分母，不应直接比较百分比。\\\\n\\\\n## 一条请求、执行与内存的组合轨迹\\\\n\\\\n以下是符号模型，时间单位为τ，容量为GiB，不是设备实测。窗口为 `[0,40)`，假定主机与设备时间已经在同一可比较坐标上，设备只展示一个顺序队列。\\\\n\\\\n| 层 | 事件与身份 |\\\\n|---|---|\\\\n| host | normalize `[0,2)`；linear入队 `[2,3)`；attention入队 `[3,4)`；标量读取 `[4,24)`；采样/序列化 `[24,28)` |\\\\n| 提交关系 | linear提交关联K1；attention提交关联K2；入队返回不代表完成 |\\\\n| device | K1为linear融合kernel `[6,14)`，共同实现gemm与bias；K2为attention `[14,22)` |\\\\n| counter | 若只覆盖整个执行范围，则保留聚合身份，不拆成两个kernel的贡献 |\\\\n| storage | weights 6 `[0,40)`；compile workspace 3 `[0,5)`；temp 2 `[6,14)`；KV 4 `[14,40)` |\\\\n\\\\nkernel并集为 `[6,22)`，长度16τ，区间和也为16τ。host范围并集为28τ，包含标量读取等待；主机与设备观测区间的联合并集仍为28τ。把28与16相加会得到44τ，重复计算了重叠时间。`[22,24)` 是模型中读取尚未返回的尾部，但没有额外事件时，不能仅凭这2τ断言发生了某个具体CPU操作；`[28,40)` 同样保留未解释状态。\\\\n\\\\nK1时长8τ，可以声明gemm和bias各分4τ，K2分给attention 8τ，总计16τ。若把K1分别完整计给gemm与bias，再加K2，就得到24τ。若另一个队列在 `[10,18)` 执行K3，则kernel区间和变成24τ，并集仍为16τ；合法分摊应守恒到24τ，而不是强行压成16τ。\\\\n\\\\nstorage活跃容量依次为 `[0,5)` 的9、`[5,6)` 的6、`[6,14)` 的8和 `[14,40)` 的10，峰值10 GiB。temp另有一个 `[8,14)` 的视图时，物理容量不增加。在8τ，正确容量为weights 6加temp 2，共8 GiB；按句柄重复计temp会得到10 GiB。错误曲线的全窗口峰值仍是10 GiB，恰好与正确峰值相同，因此只比较全窗口峰值会漏掉错误。改查 `[8,14)`，正确峰值8与错误峰值10便能区分；逐时容量参考也能发现该差异。\\\\n\\\\n若诊断性引用保留让temp的保护期持续到18，便与KV重叠，峰值升至12。该变化描述诊断条件下的生命周期，不证明普通运行的峰值也是12。在14τ释放temp并建立KV，半开区间不会制造两者同时存活；但真实设备复用仍要确认最后消费者完成。若temp的最后消费者完成于14，而存储在13就交给下一次写入，即使容量曲线看似更低，也已违反复用条件。\\\\n\\\\n这条轨迹同时连接请求消费、提交、融合、设备执行和驻留。改变求值频率可能减少固定主机成本，却延长temp保护时间；改变融合边界可能减少中间写读，却改变临时状态和归属粒度。选择需要在同一候选、同一负载与完成边界下重新列账。\\\\n\\\\n## 竞争解释、区分实验与选择修正\\\\n\\\\n| 观测 | 竞争解释 | 区分实验与预测 | 反证后的修正 |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| 每token出现增长的concatenate | 复制历史、惰性构图、元数据路径、融合或采集缺失 | 固定输出语义，记录shape和实际复制；预分配后若历史复制成立，相应字节增长应减少 | 无对应执行或字节证据时，降低历史复制解释的置信度 |\\\\n| 首次每种shape有长段 | 编译、guard变体、加载、首次分配或autotune | 同签名重复，再分别改变guard相关条件，观察新产物与首次成本 | 同签名仍持续长时，编译不能解释全部 |\\\\n| scalar extraction后出现空洞 | 设备完成等待、锁、Python处理或采集扰动 | 移动读取边界，比较设备工作量、等待位置和最终完成 | 只移动等待而输出不提前，不能称为计算加速 |\\\\n| 算子时间和大于墙钟 | 跨队列重叠、祖先inclusive范围、融合重复归属或时钟错误 | 分别恢复实例，算区间和与并集，核查祖先和shared关系 | 无重叠时转查重复归属与时钟，而非继续声称并发 |\\\\n| active下降而reserved不降 | 缓存保留、碎片、在途读者或外部分配 | 在相同完成边界减少同时存活对象，并对齐A、R、D口径 | 差额未分类前保留未知，不能直接宣称泄漏 |\\\\n| 两种内存统计的全窗口峰值相同 | 曲线确实相同，或局部错误被另一阶段峰值遮蔽 | 在别名重叠阶段比较曲线，独立按storage去重；保持其他阶段不变 | 局部容量不同即推翻统计等价，不能以全局峰值相同关闭问题 |\\\\n| capture缺少预期工作 | 未求值、窗口错误、产物不匹配或工具覆盖不足 | 覆盖明确求值和消费边界，确认执行身份 | 缺失事件不等于零工作；必要时降低结论精度 |\\\\n| Trainium runtime区域很长 | 主机等待、加载、数据供给或设备指令受限 | 用匹配NEFF的设备trace区分DMA、计算和依赖 | 系统调用没有对应片上证据时保留运行时解释 |\\\\n| CPU低IPC | 工作集、依赖、分支、调度或计数范围混杂 | 固定任务，分别改变工作集与线程预算，并检查事件共同运行范围 | 单个比值不能确定缓存层或GPU原因 |\\\\n\\\\n例如，最初认为concatenate每步复制完整历史，但随后只发现host图构造增长，没有相应复制或shape证据。此时应把原解释降级。再固定每个外层迭代的求值边界：若设备工作直到求值才出现，支持定义与执行边界解释；若真实历史读取字节仍随长度增长，复制解释才重新获得支持。预分配若改善端到端时间，却没有出现预测的流量下降，应保留候选收益并修正原因。\\\\n\\\\n工具选择允许反转：稳定形状、频繁小提交时，减少提交的预测更值得验证；设备已持续繁忙时，同样的主机优化可能只有很小收益。并发增加后，原本有效的融合或延后求值可能因驻留和排队退化，应调整边界；目标设备缺少所需计数器时，放弃具体stall归因，保留可测的路径级结论。\\\\n\\\\n## 最小观测、独立检查与未测边界\\\\n\\\\n分层测量先保留无profiler的请求完成、失败、输入输出规模与负载条件，再用代表窗口建立框架/系统关联，最后针对少量实例取得细粒度计数。普通运行验证目标，诊断运行解释机制；不同配置的数据各自保留身份。\\\\n\\\\n工具不可用时，仍可使用客户端完成时间、主机经过时间、独立正确性参考及明确完成边界的结果。若某接口确实至少要搬运 `Bmin` 字节，完整路径时间为T，则实际平均接口流量至少为 `Bmin/T`；超过可信上界时，应核查\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 4500], [8000, 12000]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 15216, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 8500, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"Ranked 4000-character windows by current entry title/tags/questions and algorithm/mechanism keywords; ties retain source order.\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"knowledge/tools/statistical-experiments.md\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"908b3588a6fa20bb1f2aed9f5db51c4b462953d79f8944cdbcfea7141c74644f\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# K-TOOLS-007：性能实验：独立重复、效应量与尾部证据\\\\n\\\\n性能结论要同时回答改了多少、波动来自哪里，以及结论适用于哪组条件。更多计时样本只有在增加了与问题相关的信息时才提高可信度；同一进程内反复测量不能自动替代重启、重新构建或不同时间段的重复。\\\\n\\\\n## 先固定比较的对象\\\\n\\\\n声明比较的是冷启动、稳态单请求、固定到达率服务，还是容量边界。版本、硬件与配额、模型、输入/输出分布、缓存条件、质量标准和测量事件必须一致。把预打包移出计时是可以研究的稳态设定，但需要另报一次性成本；它不能直接支持冷启动更快的结论。\\\\n\\\\n对于越小越好的延迟，既可以报告差值 A−B，也可以报告比值 A/B，但要说明用的是均值、分位数还是每轮比值的聚合。均值的比值、比值的均值与分位数的比值不是同一估计量。吞吐也要包含完成窗口、失败和未完成工作，而不是只选快速成功的请求。\\\\n\\\\n## 重复的层级\\\\n\\\\n一次实验包含环境/时间段、进程或模型实例、请求/迭代等层级。布局、编译、NUMA、热状态和后台竞争可以在不同层级引入变化。[效应量置信区间研究](../sources/S-STATS.md) §6–7 将这种层级变化与重复次数、比值区间连接起来；不能把其假设之外的任意轨迹直接代入公式。\\\\n\\\\n如果只有进程内反复采样，而进程间差异很大，继续增加内层重复会得到看似稳定但覆盖范围很窄的均值。先用少量分层试验辨别主要变异，再把预算投到有效层级。稳态预热规则需要事先确定或用独立预实验建立；若系统始终存在周期和漂移，应报告这种行为，而非挑一段最快区间称为稳态。\\\\n\\\\n## 配对、区组与区间\\\\n\\\\n对可重复的请求轨迹，可以在同一个时间区组内运行 A/B，并随机或均衡安排先后，控制环境漂移。配对的单位应是独立运行或区组，而不是把同一运行里强相关的每个 token 当作独立样本。若两方案会改变后续生成内容，应区分固定前缀计算对照与真实生成质量/性能对照。\\\\n\\\\n在独立配对差值 dⱼ 近似满足相应 t 区间条件时，均值差的区间为 d̄±t·s𝒹/√n。设定 16 个独立区组，平均降低 2 ms、差值样本标准差为 1 ms，使用自由度 15 的双侧 95% 临界值约 2.131，区间约为 [1.467,2.533] ms。这是给定统计量的算例；它既不证明某实现有该收益，也不是“未来单请求延迟落在其中的概率”。\\\\n\\\\n层级 bootstrap 应保留实际层级与配对关系。时间相关的数据需要考虑成块重采样或更高层独立重复，不能随机打散相关结构后制造很窄的区间。少量独立块、强漂移、极端长尾会限制区间可信度；无论用解析方法还是重采样，都需要说明独立性、平稳性与样本范围。\\\\n\\\\n## 尾延迟与失败不能被均值掩盖\\\\n\\\\np99 依赖尾部的少量样本。100 个请求的经验 p99 只有很有限的尾部信息，重复报告多个小数位不会增加精度。超时是被删失或失败的观测，不应悄悄删除；如果 SLO 定义要求在 deadline 内成功，超时和质量失败应按该定义计入。\\\\n\\\\n对固定阈值的超限率，假设 n 个独立、同分布请求且观察到零超限，单侧置信度 1−α 的上界为 1−α^(1/n)，来自零超限概率 (1−q)ⁿ。n=100、α=0.05 时上界约 2.95%；所以零失败 100 次并不能支持真实超限率低于 1% 的同等置信结论。这个二项式算例在突发相关、负载漂移或选择性停止时不能照搬。\\\\n\\\\n服务试验还应展示 offered load、队列增长、完成数与错误数。有限时间内的 goodput 不代表长期稳定；若队列持续增长，测量窗口结束时尚未完成的请求是关键证据。\\\\n\\\\n## 搜索后的验证与停止条件\\\\n\\\\n从很多候选中挑最好的结果，会同时挑中有利噪声。探索用的轨迹、形状与调参集应与最终保留验证分开；确定候选后冻结代码和配置，在独立运行上重测，并报告试过的候选范围。失败的正确性检查不能因为性能好而被排除。\\\\n\\\\n停止条件围绕实际决策设定：例如在质量通过且 SLO 不退化的前提下，收益是否超过值得维护的最小幅度。区间跨过决策边界时，证据不足以决定；应增加有效重复或说明未区分，而不是把单次最好值当成结论。持续查看结果直到恰好显著再停止，会改变统计含义，需要预先设计或使用相应的序贯方法。\\\\n\\\\n发布结论保留原始事件、运行身份、失败样本、聚合定义及不确定性。一次局部 kernel 对照仅支持该 shape 与条件；知识库是否提高 Agent 设计能力，还需要固定任务、模型和预算，对比旧 base、扩充 base 与无知识条件，并隔离各自运行学习。\\\\n\\\\n## 针对知识库作用安排受控构建实验\\\\n\\\\n下面是研究者可选择的对照设计，统计重复原则受上述固定来源支持，具体 Agent 条件不归称为来源论文的实验，也不构成 Agent 构建时必须执行的流程。研究知识条件差异时，可比较无知识、旧 seed、扩充 seed；研究运行学习时，可以另设 learned 条件。每组固定实际角色模型、任务语义、可用工具、基础代码起点、外部资料权限和预算口径，并在批次开始前冻结知识版本与评价器。各组拥有独立的案例与发布状态，防止先运行的组把经验传给后运行的组。\\\\n\\\\n主要结果包括固定预算内完整引擎的成功交付率、到第一个合格系统的成本、到目标性能的成本、以及合格系统的端到端表现。固定预算完成率中，未交付均计为未成功并保留原因。若另分析到达合格系统的时间，仍可能完成、且仅因预先统一的时间窗口结束而停止的运行，可以记为行政性右删失；崩溃或不可恢复失败应另列失败事件，不能任意按独立删失处理。其他资源预算导致的停止也需解释删失机制。不能只平均成功任务的完成时间而不说明选择范围。模型生成存在随机性，独立重复的单位是完整构建运行，而不是一个运行中的多个工作项。\\\\n\\\\n检索命中、正文读取和知识使用声明用于检查访问链路；预期设计改变是否进入实现，需要单独核对。若扩充组减少无效实验且在相同验收标准下实测总成本或到达合格系统的成本下降，即使未提高最终吞吐，也可以支持构建成本改善；仅减少实验次数并不充分，因为剩余实验可能更昂贵。若交付率提高却消耗更多资源，则应展示相应权衡，不能只报告最好的一条轨迹。\\\\n\\\\n扩充内容中的示范任务与算例不应直接成为唯一最终测试集。开发场景与独立保留场景分开，按模型结构、硬件能力、负载和状态交互说明哪些条件发生了变化。硬件不能全部交叉时报告实际测试子集，避免将一个设备的结果外推为跨平台收益。\\\\n\\\\n## 检查测量链是否会接受不可能的提升\\\\n\\\\n性能测量的负对照保持任务标准不变，主动制造应该使结果失格的轨迹：缺失响应却缩短总时间、提前结束测量仍有在途请求、只保留快请求、在 benchmark 中跳过真实模型路径。测量应拒绝这些轨迹或明确记录缺失/失败，而不是给出更好的成功分数。\\\\n\\\\n计量完成点与质量完成点应绑定到同一批请求和候选版本。profiling 的同步、额外复制或影子参考会扰动执行；用于诊断的计数与最终正常路径的性能分开报告。原始数据若不足以重建规定的统计量，结论是未测得，不以另一个聚合量替代。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- infraagents:provenance -->\\\\n\\\\n## 来源与推导\\\\n\\\\n- [S-STATS：Quantifying Performance Changes with Effect The collected data can then be copied to any system and analyzed\\\\n\\\\nlater.\\\\nThe CLI is distributed in the Target directory of the standard Nsight Systems\\\\n\\\\ndownload package.\\\\nIf you wish to run the CLI without root (recommended mode), you will want to\\\\n\\\\ninstall in a directory where you have full access.\\\\nNote that you must run the CLI on Windows as administrator.\\\\nCommand Line Options\\\\n\\\\nThe Nsight Systems command lines can have one of two forms:\\\\nnsys\\\\n[\\\\nglobal_option\\\\n]\\\\nor\\\\nnsys\\\\n[\\\\ncommand_switch\\\\n][\\\\noptional\\\\ncommand_switch_options\\\\n][\\\\napplication\\\\n]\\\\n[\\\\noptional\\\\napplication_options\\\\n]\\\\nAll command line options are case sensitive. For command switch options, when short options are used, the parameters should follow the switch after a space; e.g.\\\\n-s\\\\nprocess-tree\\\\n. When long options are used, the switch should be followed by an equal sign and then the parameter(s); e.g.\\\\n--sample=process-tree\\\\n.\\\\nFor this version of Nsight Systems, if you launch a process from the command line to begin analysis, the launched process will be terminated when collection is complete, including runs with\\\\n--duration\\\\nset, unless the user specifies the\\\\n--kill\\\\nnone\\\\noption (details below). The exception is that if the user uses NVTX, cudaProfilerStart/Stop, or hotkeys to control the duration, the application will continue unless\\\\n--kill\\\\nis set.\\\\nThe Nsight Systems CLI supports concurrent analysis by using sessions. Each Nsight Systems session is defined by a sequence of CLI commands that define one or more collections (e.g. when and what data is collected). A session begins with either a start, launch, or profile command. A session ends with a shutdown command, when a profile command terminates, or, if requested, when all the process tree(s) launched in the session exit. Multiple sessions can run concurrently on the same system.\\\\nCLI Global Options\\\\n\\\\nShort\\\\nLong\\\\nDescription\\\\n-h\\\\n--help\\\\nHelp message providing information about available command switches and their options.\\\\n-v\\\\n--version\\\\nOutput Nsight Systems CLI version information.\\\\nCLI Command Switches\\\\n\\\\nThe Nsight Systems command line interface can be used in two modes. Each D3D device in each process is associated with one or more contexts. Graphics, compute, and copy commands that the profiled application uses are associated with a context, batched in a command buffer, and pushed into the relevant queue associated with that context.\\\\nNsight Systems can capture the state of these queues during the trace session.\\\\nEnabling the “Collect additional range of ETW events” option will also capture extended DxgKrnl events from the\\\\nMicrosoft-Windows-DxgKrnl\\\\nprovider, such as context status, allocations, sync wait, signal events, etc.\\\\nA command buffer in a WDDM queues may have one the following types:\\\\nRender\\\\nDeferred\\\\nSystem\\\\nMMIOFlip\\\\nWait\\\\nSignal\\\\nDevice\\\\nSoftware\\\\nIt may also be marked as a Present buffer, indicating that the application has finished rendering and requests to display the source surface.\\\\nSee the Microsoft documentation for the WDDM architecture and the DXGKETW_QUEUE_PACKET_TYPE enumeration.\\\\nTo retain the .etl trace files captured, so that they can be viewed in other tools (e.g. GPUView), change the “Save ETW log files in project folder” option under “Profile Behavior” in Nsight Systems’s global Options dialog. The .etl files will appear in the same folder as the .nsys-rep file, accessible by right-clicking the report in the Project Explorer and choosing “Show in Folder…”. Data collected from each ETW provider will appear in its own .etl file, and an additional .etl file named “Report XX-Merged-*.etl”, containing the events from all captured sources, will be created as well.\\\\nWDDM HW Scheduler\\\\n\\\\nWhen GPU Hardware Scheduling is enabled in Windows 10 or newer version, the Windows Display Driver Model (WDDM) uses the DxgKrnl ETW provider to expose report of NVIDIA GPUs’ hardware scheduling context switches.\\\\nNsight Systems can capture these context switch events, and display under the GPUs in the timeline rows titled WDDM HW Scheduler - [HW Queue type]. The ranges under each queue will show the process name and PID assoicated with the GPU work during the time period.\\\\nThe events will be captured if GPU Hardware Scheduling is enabled in the Windows System Display settings, and “Collect WDDM Trace” is enabled in the Nsight Systems Project Settings.\\\\nVulkan API Trace\\\\n\\\\nVulkan Overview\\\\n\\\\nVulkan is a low-overhead, cross-platform 3D graphics and compute API, targeting a wide variety of devices from PCs to mobile phones and embedded platforms. The Vulkan API is defined by the Khronos Group. Information about Vulkan and the Khronos Group can be found at the\\\\nKhronos Vulkan Site\\\\n.\\\\nNsight Systems can capture information about Vulkan usage by the profiled process. This includes capturing the execution time of Vulkan API functions, corresponding GPU workloads, debug util labels, and frame durations. Vulkan profiling is supported on both Windows and x86 Linux operating systems.\\\\nThe Command Buffer Creation row displays time periods when command buffers were being created. This enables developers to improve their application’s multi-threaded command buffer creation. Command buffer creation time period is measured between the call to\\\\nvkBeginCommandBuffer\\\\nand the call to\\\\nvkEndCommandBuffer\\\\n.\\\\nA Queue row is displayed for each Vulkan queue created by the profiled application. The API sub-row displays time periods where\\\\nvkQueueSubmit\\\\nwas called. The GPU Workload sub-row displays time periods where workloads were executed by the GPU.\\\\nIn addition, you can see\\\\nVulkan debug util labels\\\\non both the CPU and the GPU.\\\\nClicking on a GPU workload highlights the corresponding\\\\nvkQueueSubmit\\\\ncall, and vice versa.\\\\nThe Vulkan Memory Operations row contains an aggregation of all the Vulkan host-side memory operations, such as host-blocking writes and reads or non-persistent map-unmap ranges.\\\\nThe row is separated into sub-rows by heap index and memory type - the tooltip for each row and the ranges inside show the\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 168000:180000]\\\\n the “Insert NVTX Marker hotkey” option it is possible\\\\n\\\\nto add NVTX markers to a running non-console applications by pressing the\\\\n\\\\nF11 key. These will appear in the report under the NVTX Domain named “HotKey\\\\n\\\\nmarkers”.\\\\nTypically calls to NVTX functions can be left in the source code even if the\\\\n\\\\napplication is not being built for profiling purposes, since the overhead is\\\\n\\\\nvery low when the profiler is not attached.\\\\nNVTX is not intended to annotate very small pieces of code that are being called\\\\n\\\\nvery frequently. A good rule of thumb to use: if code being annotated usually\\\\n\\\\ntakes less than 1 microsecond to execute, adding an NVTX range around this code\\\\n\\\\nshould be done carefully.\\\\nNote\\\\nRange annotations should be matched carefully. If many ranges are opened but\\\\n\\\\nnot closed, Nsight Systems has no meaningful way to visualize it. A rule of\\\\n\\\\nthumb is to not have more than a couple dozen ranges open at any point in\\\\n\\\\ntime. Values are in the [1,100] range.\\\\nib-switch-congestion-threshold-high\\\\nThis defines the high threshold for InfiniBand switch egress port queue size.\\\\n\\\\nWhen a packet enters an InfiniBand switch, its data is stored at an ingress port\\\\n\\\\nbuffer. A pointer to the packet’s data is inserted into the egress port’s queue,\\\\n\\\\nfrom which the packet will be exiting the switch. At that point, the threshold\\\\n\\\\ngiven by this command switch is compared to the egress queue data size. If the\\\\n\\\\nqueue data size exceeds the threshold, a congestion event is reported. The\\\\n\\\\nthreshold is given in percent of the ingress port size. An egress port queue can\\\\n\\\\npoint to data coming from multiple ingress port buffers, therefore the threshold\\\\n\\\\ncan be bigger than 100%. Values are in the [1,1023] range\\\\nInfiniBand Network Information\\\\n\\\\nOverview\\\\nBy default, Nsight Systems displays low-level identifiers like LIDs (Local\\\\n\\\\nIdentifiers) and GUIDs (Globally Unique Identifiers). Default is the same name and path as the .qdstrm file.\\\\nLaunch Processes in Stopped State\\\\n\\\\nIn many cases, it is important to profile an application from the very beginning of its execution. When launching processes, Nsight Systems takes care of it by making sure that the profiling session is fully initialized before making the\\\\nexec()\\\\nsystem call on Linux.\\\\nIf the process launch capabilities of Nsight Systems are not sufficient, the application should be launched manually, and the profiler should be configured to attach to the already launched process. One approach would be to call\\\\nsleep()\\\\nsomewhere early in the application code, which would provide time for the user to attach to the process in Nsight Systems Embedded Platforms Edition, but there are two other more convenient mechanisms that can be used on Linux, without the need to recompile the application. (Note that the rest of this section is only applicable to Linux-based target devices.)\\\\nBoth mechanisms ensure that between the time the process is created (and therefore its PID is known) and the time any of the application’s code is called, the process is stopped and waits for a signal to be delivered before continuing.\\\\nLD_PRELOAD\\\\n\\\\nThe first mechanism uses\\\\nLD_PRELOAD\\\\nenvironment variable. Although not limited to\\\\ntracing, context propagation allows [traces](../signals/traces/) to build causal\\\\ninformation about a system across services that are arbitrarily distributed\\\\nacross process and network boundaries.\\\\n\\\\nTo understand context propagation, you need to understand two separate concepts:\\\\ncontext and propagation.\\\\n\\\\n## Context\\\\n\\\\nContext is an object that contains the information for the sending and receiving\\\\nservice, or [execution unit](/docs/specs/otel/glossary/#execution-unit), to\\\\ncorrelate one signal with another.\\\\n\\\\nWhen Service A calls Service B, Service A includes a trace ID and a span ID as\\\\npart of the context. Service B uses these values to create a new span that\\\\nbelongs to the same trace, setting the span from Service A as its parent. This\\\\nmakes it possible to track the full flow of a request across service boundaries.\\\\n\\\\n## Propagation\\\\n\\\\nPropagation is the mechanism that moves context between services and processes.\\\\nIt serializes or deserializes the context object and provides the relevant\\\\ninformation to be propagated from one service to another.\\\\n\\\\nPropagation is usually handled by instrumentation libraries and is transparent\\\\nto the user. In the event that you need to manually propagate context, you can\\\\nuse the [Propagators API](/docs/specs/otel/context/api-propagators/).\\\\n\\\\nOpenTelemetry maintains several official propagators. The default propagator\\\\nuses the headers specified by the\\\\n[W3C TraceContext](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) specification.\\\\n\\\\n## Example\\\\n\\\\nA service called `Frontend` that provides different HTTP endpoints such as\\\\n`POST /cart/add` and `GET /checkout/` reaches out to a downstream service\\\\n`Product Catalog` via an HTTP endpoint `GET /product` to receive details on\\\\nproducts that a user wants to add to the cart or that are part of the checkout.\\\\nTo understand activities in the `Product Catalog` service within the context of\\\\nrequests coming from `Frontend`, the context (here: Trace ID and Span ID as\\\\n\\\\\\\"Parent ID\\\\\\\") is propagated using the `traceparent` header as it is defined in\\\\nthe W3C TraceContext specification. This means the IDs are embedded in the\\\\nfields of the header:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\n<version>-<trace-id>-<parent-id>-<trace-flags>\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFor example:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\n00-a0892f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-f03067aa0ba902b7-01\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Traces\\\\n\\\\nAs mentioned, context propagation allows traces to build causal information\\\\nacross services. In this example, the two calls to the HTTP endpoint\\\\n`GET /product` of service `Product Catalog` can be correlated with their\\\\nupstream calls in service `Frontend` by extracting the remote context from the\\\\n`traceparent` header and injecting it into the local context to set the Trace ID\\\\nand Parent ID. With that, it is possible in a [backend](/ecosystem/vendors) like\\\\n[Jaeger](https://jaegertracing.io) to see two requests as spans of one trace.\\\\n\\\\n![Context propagation example showing trace correlation across services](context-propagation-example.svg)\\\\n\\\\n### Logs\\\\n\\\\nOpenTelemetry SDKs are able to automatically correlate logs with traces. This\\\\nmeans they can inject context (Trace ID, Span ID) into a log record. This not\\\\nonly enables you to see logs in the context of the trace and span they belong\\\\nto, but it also enables you to see logs that belong together across service or\\\\nexecution unit boundaries.\\\\n\\\\n### Metrics\\\\n\\\\nIn the case of metrics, context propagation enables you to aggregate\\\\nmeasurements in that context. For example, instead of only looking at the\\\\nresponse time of all the `GET /product` requests, you can also get metrics for\\\\ncombinations of `POST /cart/add > GET /product` and\\\\n`GET /checkout < GET /product`.\\\\n\\\\n| Name                            | Calls Per Second | Average Response Time |\\\\n| ------------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------- |\\\\n| `* > GET /product`              | 370              | 300ms                 |\\\\n| `POST /card/add > GET /product` | 330              | 130ms                 |\\\\n| `GET /checkout > GET /product`  | 40               | 1703ms                |\\\\n\\\\n## Custom Context Propagation\\\\n\\\\nFor most use cases, you will find\\\\n[instrumentation libraries or native library instrumentation](/docs/concepts/instrumentation/libraries/)\\\\nthat handle the context propagation for you. In some cases no such support is\\\\navailable and you want to create that support for yourself. To do so you need to\\\\nleverage the previously mentioned Propagators API:\\\\n\\\\n- On the side of the sender, the context is\\\\n  [injected](/docs/specs/otel/context/api-propagators/#inject) into the carrier,\\\\n  for example, into the headers of an HTTP request. In other cases, you need to\\\\n  find a place that can store metadata for your request.\\\\n- On the receiving side, the context is\\\\n  [extracted](/docs/specs/otel/context/api-propagators/#extract) from the\\\\n  carrier. Again, in the case of HTTP, this is retrieved from the headers. In\\\\n  other cases, you pick the place you chose on the sending side to store the\\\\n  context.\\\\n\\\\nNote that it is possible to propagate context in protocols that do not have a\\\\ndedicated field for metadata, but you have to make sure that on the receiving\\\\nside they are extracted and removed before the data is processed, otherwise you\\\\nmay create undefined behavior.\\\\n\\\\nFor the following languages a step-by-step tutorial exists for custom context\\\\npropagation:\\\\n\\\\n- [Erlang](/docs/languages/erlang/propagation/#manual-context-propagation)\\\\n- [JavaScript](/docs/languages/js/propagation/#manual-context-propagation)\\\\n- [PHP](/docs/languages/php/propagation/#manual-context-propagation)\\\\n- [Python](/docs/languages/python/propagation/#manual-context-propagation)\\\\n\\\\n## Security best practices\\\\n\\\\nPropagation involves sending and receiving data across service boundaries, which\\\\ncan have security implications.\\\\n\\\\n### External services\\\\n\\\\nWhen your service interacts with external services (services you do not own or\\\\ntrust), consider the following:\\\\n\\\\n- **Incoming context**: Be cautious when accepting context from external\\\\n  sources. Malicious actors could send forged trace headers to manipulate your\\\\n  tracing data or potentially exploit vulnerabilities in context parsing. You\\\\n  might want to ignore or sanitize incoming context from untrusted sources.\\\\n- **Outgoing context**: Be mindful of what you propagate to external services.\\\\n  Internal trace IDs, span IDs, or baggage items might reveal sensitive\\\\n  information about your internal architecture or business logic. You may want\\\\n  to configure your propagators to not send context to external or public-facing\\\\n  endpoints.\\\\n\\\\n### Baggage\\\\n\\\\n[Baggage](../signals/baggage/) allows you to propagate arbitrary key-value\\\\npairs. Since this data is propagated across service boundaries, avoid putting\\\\nsensitive information (like user credentials, API keys, or PII) in baggage, as\\\\nit might be logged or sent to untrusted downstream services.\\\\n\\\\n## Support in Language SDKs\\\\n\\\\nFor the individual language-specific implementations of the OpenTelemetry API &\\\\nSDK, you will find details on the support of context propagation in the\\\\nrespective documentation pages:\\\\n\\\\n- [C++](/docs/languages/cpp/instrumentation/#context-propagation)\\\\n- .NET\\\\n- [Erlang](/docs/languages/erlang/propagation/)\\\\n- [Go](/docs/languages/go/instrumentation/#propagators-and-context)\\\\n- [Java](/docs/languages/java/api/#context-api)\\\\n- [JavaScript](/docs/languages/js/propagation/)\\\\n- [PHP](/docs/languages/php/propagation/)\\\\n- [Python](/docs/languages/python/propagation/)\\\\n- [Ruby](/docs/languages/ruby/instrumentation/#context-propagation)\\\\n- Rust\\\\n- Swift\\\\n\\\\n> [!IMPORTANT] Help wanted\\\\n>\\\\n> For languages .NET, Rust, and Swift, the language-specific documentation for\\\\n> context propagation is missing. Host Memory\\\\n\\\\nThe runtime provides functions to allow the use of\\\\npage-locked\\\\n(also known as\\\\npinned\\\\n) host memory (as opposed to regular pageable host memory allocated by\\\\nmalloc()\\\\n):\\\\ncudaHostAlloc()\\\\nand\\\\ncudaFreeHost()\\\\nallocate and free page-locked host memory;\\\\ncudaHostRegister()\\\\npage-locks a range of memory allocated by\\\\nmalloc()\\\\n(see reference manual for limitations).\\\\nUsing page-locked host memory has several benefits:\\\\nCopies between page-locked host memory and device memory can be performed concurrently with kernel execution for some devices as mentioned in\\\\nAsynchronous Concurrent Execution\\\\n.\\\\nOn some devices, page-locked host memory can be mapped into the address space of the device, eliminating the need to copy it to or from device memory as detailed in\\\\nMapped Memory\\\\n.\\\\nOn systems with a front-side bus, bandwidth between host memory and device memory is higher if host memory is allocated as page-locked and even higher if in addition it is allocated as write-combining as described in\\\\nWrite-Combining Memory\\\\n.\\\\nNote\\\\nPage-locked host memory is not cached on non I/O coherent Tegra devices. Also,\\\\ncudaHostRegister()\\\\nis not supported on non I/O coherent Tegra devices.\\\\nThe simple zero-copy CUDA sample comes with a detailed document on the page-locked memory APIs.\\\\n3.2.6.1.\\\\nPortable Memory\\\\n\\\\nA block of page-locked memory can be used in conjunction with any device in the system (see\\\\nMulti-Device System\\\\nfor more details on multi-device systems), but by default, the benefits of using page-locked memory described above are only available in conjunction with the device that was current when the block was allocated (and with all devices sharing the same unified address space, if any, as described in\\\\nUnified Virtual Address Space\\\\n). To make these advantages available to all devices, the block needs to be allocated by passing the flag\\\\ncudaHostAllocPortable\\\\nto\\\\ncudaHostAlloc()\\\\nor page-locked by passing the flag\\\\ncudaHostRegisterPortable\\\\nto\\\\ncudaHostRegister()\\\\n.\\\\n3.2.6.2.\\\\nWrite-Combining Memory\\\\n\\\\nBy default page-locked host memory is allocated as cacheable. It can optionally be allocated as\\\\nwrite-combining\\\\ninstead by passing flag\\\\ncudaHostAllocWriteCombined\\\\nto\\\\ncudaHostAlloc()\\\\n. Write-combining memory frees up the host’s L1 and L2 cache resources, making more cache available to the rest of the application. In addition, write-combining memory is not snooped during transfers across the PCI Express bus, which can improve transfer performance by up to 40%.\\\\nReading from write-combining memory from the host is prohibitively slow, so write-combining memory should in general be used for memory that the host only writes to.\\\\nUsing CPU atomic instructions on WC memory should be avoided because not all CPU implementations guarantee that functionality.\\\\n3.2.6.3.\\\\nMapped Memory\\\\n\\\\nA block of page-locked host memory can also be mapped into the address space of the device by passing flag\\\\ncudaHostAllocMapped\\\\nto\\\\ncudaHostAlloc()\\\\nor by passing flag\\\\ncudaHostRegisterMapped\\\\nto\\\\ncudaHostRegister()\\\\n. Therefore, switching from one execution context to another has no cost, and at every instruction issue time, a warp scheduler selects a warp that has threads ready to execute its next instruction (the\\\\nactive threads\\\\nof the warp) and issues the instruction to those threads.\\\\nIn particular, each multiprocessor has a set of 32-bit registers that are partitioned among the warps, and a\\\\nparallel data cache\\\\nor\\\\nshared memory\\\\nthat is partitioned among the thread blocks.\\\\nThe number of blocks and warps that can reside and be processed together on the multiprocessor for a given kernel depends on the amount of registers and shared memory used by the kernel and the amount of registers and shared memory available on the multiprocessor. There are also a maximum number of resident blocks and a maximum number of resident warps per multiprocessor. These limits as well the amount of registers and shared memory available on the multiprocessor are a function of the compute capability of the device and are given in\\\\nCompute Capabilities\\\\n. If there are not enough registers or shared memory available per multiprocessor to process at least one block, the kernel will fail to launch.\\\\nThe total number of warps in a block is as follows:\\\\n\\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\text{ceil}\\\\\\\\left( \\\\\\\\frac{T}{W_{size}},1 \\\\\\\\right)\\\\\\\\)\\\\nT\\\\nis the number of threads per block,\\\\nWsize\\\\nis the warp size, which is equal to 32,\\\\nceil(x, y) is equal to x rounded up to the nearest multiple of y.\\\\nThe total number of registers and total amount of shared memory allocated for a block are documented in the CUDA Occupancy Calculator provided in the CUDA Toolkit.\\\\n2\\\\nThe term\\\\nwarp-synchronous\\\\nrefers to code that implicitly assumes threads in the same warp are synchronized at every instruction.\\\\n5.\\\\nPerformance Guidelines\\\\n\\\\n5.1.\\\\nOverall Performance Optimization Strategies\\\\n\\\\nPerformance optimization revolves around four basic strategies:\\\\nMaximize parallel execution to achieve maximum utilization;\\\\nOptimize memory usage to achieve maximum memory throughput;\\\\nOptimize instruction usage to achieve maximum instruction throughput;\\\\nMinimize memory thrashing.\\\\nWhich strategies will yield the best performance gain for a particular portion of an application depends on the performance limiters for that portion; optimizing instruction usage of a kernel that is mostly limited by memory accesses will not yield any significant performance gain, for example. Optimization efforts should therefore be constantly directed by measuring and monitoring the performance limiters, for example using the CUDA profiler. Also, comparing the floating-point operation throughput or memory throughput—whichever makes more sense—of a particular kernel to the corresponding peak theoretical throughput of the device indicates how much room for improvement there is for the kernel.\\\\n5.2.\\\\nMaximize Utilization\\\\n\\\\nTo maximize utilization the application should be structured in a way that it exposes as much parallelism as possible and efficiently maps this parallelism to the various components of the system to keep them busy most of the time.\\\\n5.2.1.\\\\nApplication Level\\\\n\\\\nAt a high level, the application should maximize parallel execution between the host, the devices, and the bus connecting the host to the devices, by using asynchronous functions calls and streams as described in\\\\nAsynchronous Concurrent Execution\\\\n. It should assign to each processor the type of work it does best: serial workloads to the host; parallel workloads to the devices.\\\\nFor the parallel workloads, at points in the algorithm where parallelism is broken because some threads need to synchronize in order to share data with each other, there are two cases: Either these threads belong to the same block, in which case they should use\\\\n__syncthreads()\\\\nand share data through shared memory within the same kernel invocation, or they belong to different blocks, in which case they must share data through global memory using two separate kernel invocations, one for writing to and one for reading from global memory. The second case is much less optimal since it adds the overhead of extra kernel invocations and global memory traffic. Its occurrence should therefore be minimized by mapping the algorithm to the CUDA programming model in such a way that the computations that require inter-thread communication are performed within a single thread block as much as possible.\\\\n5.2.2.\\\\nDevice Level\\\\n\\\\nAt a lower level, the application should maximize parallel execution between the multiprocessors of a device.\\\\nMultiple kernels can execute concurrently on a device, so maximum utilization can also be achieved by using streams to enable enough kernels to execute concurrently as described in\\\\nAsynchronous Concurrent Execution\\\\n.\\\\n5.2.3.\\\\nMultiprocessor Level\\\\n\\\\nAt an even lower level, the application should maximize parallel execution between the various functional units within a multiprocessor.\\\\nAs described in\\\\nHardware Multithreading\\\\n, a GPU multiprocessor primarily relies on thread-level parallelism to maximize utilization of its functional units. Utilization is therefore directly linked to the number of resident warps. At every instruction issue time, a warp scheduler selects an instruction that is ready to execute. This instruction can be another independent instruction of the same warp, exploiting instruction-level parallelism, or more commonly an instruction of another warp, exploiting thread-level parallelism. If a ready to execute instruction is selected it is issued to the\\\\nactive\\\\nthreads of the warp. The number of clock cycles it takes for a warp to be ready to execute its next instruction is called the\\\\nlatency\\\\n, and full utilization is achieved when all warp schedulers always have some instruction to issue for some warp at e\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 296000:304000]\\\\n.\\\\nx\\\\n;\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\nidx\\\\n<\\\\narrayCount\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\narray\\\\n[\\\\nidx\\\\n]\\\\n*=\\\\narray\\\\n[\\\\nidx\\\\n];\\\\n}\\\\n}\\\\n// Host code\\\\nint\\\\nlaunchMyKernel\\\\n(\\\\nint\\\\n*\\\\narray\\\\n,\\\\nint\\\\narrayCount\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\nint\\\\nblockSize\\\\n;\\\\n// The launch configurator returned block size\\\\nint\\\\nminGridSize\\\\n;\\\\n// The minimum grid size needed to achieve the\\\\n// maximum occupancy for a full device\\\\n// launch\\\\nint\\\\ngridSize\\\\n;\\\\n// The actual grid size needed, based on input\\\\n// size\\\\ncudaOccupancyMaxPotentialBlockSize\\\\n(\\\\n&\\\\nminGridSize\\\\n,\\\\n&\\\\nblockSize\\\\n,\\\\n(\\\\nvoid\\\\n*\\\\n)\\\\nMyKernel\\\\n,\\\\n0\\\\n,\\\\narrayCount\\\\n);\\\\n// Round up according to array size\\\\ngridSize\\\\n=\\\\n(\\\\narrayCount\\\\n+\\\\nblockSize\\\\n-\\\\n1\\\\n)\\\\n/\\\\nblockSize\\\\n;\\\\nMyKernel\\\\n<<<\\\\ngridSize\\\\n,\\\\nblockSize\\\\n>>>\\\\n(\\\\narray\\\\n,\\\\narrayCount\\\\n);\\\\ncudaDeviceSynchronize\\\\n();\\\\n// If interested, the occupancy can be calculated with\\\\n// cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor\\\\nreturn\\\\n0\\\\n;\\\\n}\\\\nThe following code sample shows how to use the cluster occupancy API to find the max number of active clusters of a given size. The Nsight Compute version of the occupancy calculator is particularly useful as a learning tool that visualizes the impact of changes to the parameters that affect occupancy (block size, registers per thread, and shared memory per thread).\\\\n5.3.\\\\nMaximize Memory Throughput\\\\n\\\\nThe first step in maximizing overall memory throughput for the application is to minimize data transfers with low bandwidth.\\\\nThat means minimizing data transfers between the host and the device, as detailed in\\\\nData Transfer between Host and Device\\\\n, since these have much lower bandwidth than data transfers between global memory and the device.\\\\nThat also means minimizing data transfers between global memory and the device by maximizing use of on-chip memory: shared memory and caches (i.e., L1 cache and L2 cache available on devices of compute capability 2.x and higher, texture cache and constant cache available on all devices).\\\\nShared memory is equivalent to a user-managed cache: The application explicitly allocates and accesses it. As illustrated in\\\\nCUDA Runtime\\\\n, a typical programming pattern is to stage data coming from device memory into shared memory; in other words, to have each thread of a block:\\\\nLoad data from device memory to shared memory,\\\\nSynchronize with all the other threads of the block so that each thread can safely read shared memory locations that were populated by different threads,\\\\nProcess the data in shared memory,\\\\nSynchronize again if necessary to make sure that shared memory has been updated with the results,\\\\nWrite the results back to device memory.\\\\nFor some applications (for example, for which global memory access patterns are data-dependent), a traditional hardware-managed cache is more appropriate to exploit data locality. As mentioned in\\\\nCompute Capability 7.x\\\\n,\\\\nCompute Capability 8.x\\\\nand\\\\nCompute Capability 9.0\\\\n, for devices of compute capability 7.x, 8.x and 9.0, the same on-chip memory is used for both L1 and shared memory, and how much of it is dedicated to L1 versus shared memory is configurable for each kernel call.\\\\nThe throughput of memory accesses by a kernel can vary by an order of magnitude depending on access pattern for each type of memory. The next step in maximizing memory throughput is therefore to organize memory accesses as optimally as possible based on the optimal memory access patterns described in\\\\nDevice Memory Accesses\\\\n. This optimization is especially important for global memory accesses as global memory bandwidth is low compared to available on-chip bandwidths and arithmetic instruction throughput, so non-optimal global memory accesses generally have a high impact on performance.\\\\n5.3.1.\\\\nData Transfer between Host and Device\\\\n\\\\nApplications should strive to minimize data transfer between the host and the device. One way to accomplish this is to move more code from the host to the device, even if that means running kernels that do not expose enough parallelism to execute on the device with full efficiency. Intermediate data structures may be created in device memory, operated on by the device, and destroyed without ever being mapped by the host or copied to host memory.\\\\nAlso, because of the overhead associated with each transfer, batching many small transfers into a single large transfer always performs better than making each transfer separately.\\\\nOn systems with a front-side bus, higher performance for data transfers between host and device is achieved by using page-locked host memory as described in\\\\nPage-Locked Host Memory\\\\n.\\\\nIn addition, when using mapped page-locked memory (\\\\nMapped Memory\\\\n), there is no need to allocate any device memory and explicitly copy data between device and host memory. Data transfers are implicitly performed each time the kernel accesses the mapped memory. For maximum performance, these memory accesses must be coalesced as with accesses to global memory (see\\\\nDevice Memory Accesses\\\\n). Assuming that they are and that the mapped memory is read or written only once, using mapped page-locked memory instead of explicit copies between device and host memory can be a win for performance.\\\\nOn integrated systems where device memory and host memory are physically the same, any copy between host and device memory is superfluous and mapped page-locked memory should be used instead. Applications may query a device is\\\\nintegrated\\\\nby checking that the integrated device property (see\\\\nDevice Enumeration\\\\n) is equal to 1.\\\\n5.3.2.\\\\nDevice Memory Accesses\\\\n\\\\nAn instruction that accesses addressable memory (i.e., global, local, shared, constant, or texture memory) might need to be re-issued multiple times depending on the distribution of the memory addresses across the threads within the warp. How the distribution affects the instruction throughput this way is specific to each type of memory and described in the following sections. For example, for global memory, as a general rule, the more scattered the addresses are, the more reduced the throughput is.\\\\nGlobal Memory\\\\nGlobal memory resides in device memory and device memory is accessed via 32-, 64-, or 128-byte memory transactions. These memory transactions must be naturally aligned: Only the 32-, 64-, or 128-byte segments of device memory that are aligned to their size (i.e., whose first address is a multiple of their size) can be read or written by memory transactions.\\\\nWhen a warp executes an instruction that accesses global memory, it coalesces the memory accesses of the threads within the warp into one or more of these memory transactions depending on the size of t\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 316000:320000]\\\\ntypes\\\\n32\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\n64\\\\nType conversions from and to 64-bit types\\\\n4\\\\n16\\\\n4\\\\n16\\\\n10\\\\n16\\\\n2\\\\n2\\\\n16\\\\nAll other type conversions\\\\n32\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\n16\\\\n16-bit DPX\\\\nMultiple instruct.\\\\n128\\\\n32-bit DPX\\\\nMultiple instruct.\\\\n64\\\\nOther instructions and functions are implemented on top of the native instructions. It is therefore recommended to invoke\\\\nrsqrtf()\\\\ndirectly where desired.\\\\nSingle-Precision Floating-Point Square Root\\\\nSingle-precision floating-point square root is implemented as a reciprocal square root followed by a reciprocal instead of a reciprocal square root followed by a multiplication so that it gives correct results for 0 and infinity.\\\\nSine and Cosine\\\\nsinf(x)\\\\n,\\\\ncosf(x)\\\\n,\\\\ntanf(x)\\\\n,\\\\nsincosf(x)\\\\n, and corresponding double-precision instructions are much more expensive and even more so if the argument x is large in magnitude.\\\\nMore precisely, the argument reduction code (see\\\\nMathematical Functions\\\\nfor implementation) comprises two code paths referred to as the fast path and the slow path, respectively.\\\\nThe fast path is used for arguments sufficiently small in magnitude and essentially consists of a few multiply-add operations. The slow path is used for arguments large in magnitude and consists of lengthy computations required to achieve correct results over the entire argument range.\\\\nAt present, the argument reduction code for the trigonometric functions selects the fast path for arguments whose magnitude is less than\\\\n105615.0f\\\\nfor the single-precision functions, and less than\\\\n2147483648.0\\\\nfor the double-precision functions.\\\\nAs the slow path requires more registers than the fast path, an attempt has been made to reduce register pressure in the slow path by storing some intermediate variables in local memory, which may affect performance because of local memory high latency and bandwidth (see\\\\nDevice Memory Accesses\\\\n). At present, 28 bytes of local memory are used by single-precision functions, and 44 bytes are used by double-precision functions. However, the exact amount is subject to change.\\\\nDue to the lengthy computations and use of local memory in the slow path, the throughput of these trigonometric functions is lower by one order of magnitude when the slow path reduction is required as opposed to the fast path reduction.\\\\nInteger Arithmetic\\\\nInteger division and modulo operation are costly as they compile to up to 20 instructions. They can be replaced with bitwise operations in some cases: If\\\\nn\\\\nis a power of 2, (\\\\ni/n\\\\n) is equivalent to\\\\n(i>>log2(n))\\\\nand\\\\n(i%n)\\\\nis equivalent to (\\\\ni&(n-1)\\\\n); the compiler will perform these conversions if\\\\nn\\\\nis literal.\\\\n__brev\\\\nand\\\\n__popc\\\\nmap to a si\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 324000:332000]\\\\nrecommend the following:\\\\nTry to size your allocation to the problem at hand. Don’t try to allocate all available memory with\\\\ncudaMalloc\\\\n/\\\\ncudaMallocHost\\\\n/\\\\ncuMemCreate\\\\n, as this forces memory to be resident immediately and prevents other applications from being able to use that memory. This can put more pressure on operating system schedulers, or just prevent other applications using the same GPU from running entirely.\\\\nTry to allocate memory in appropriately sized allocations early in the application and allocations only when the application does not have any use for it. Reduce the number of\\\\ncudaMalloc\\\\n+\\\\ncudaFree\\\\ncalls in the application, especially in performance-critical regions.\\\\nIf an application cannot allocate enough device memory, consider falling back on other memory types such as\\\\ncudaMallocHost\\\\nor\\\\ncudaMallocManaged\\\\n, which may not be as performant, but will enable the application to make progress.\\\\nFor platforms that support the feature,\\\\ncudaMallocManaged\\\\nallows for oversubscription, and with the correct\\\\ncudaMemAdvise\\\\npolicies enabled, will allow the application to retain most if not all the performance of\\\\ncudaMalloc\\\\n.\\\\ncudaMallocManaged\\\\nalso won’t force an allocation to be resident until it is needed or prefetched, reducing the overall pressure on the operating system schedulers and better enabling multi-tenet use cases.\\\\n3\\\\n128 for __nv_bfloat16\\\\n4\\\\n8 for GeForce GPUs, except for Titan GPUs\\\\n5\\\\n2 for compute capability 7.5 GPUs\\\\n6\\\\n32 for extended-precision\\\\n7\\\\n32 for GeForce GPUs, except for Titan GPUs\\\\n8\\\\n16 for compute capabilities 7.5 GPUs\\\\n9\\\\n8 for GeForce GPUs, except for Titan GPUs\\\\n10\\\\n2 for compute capabilities 7.5 GPUs\\\\n6.\\\\nCUDA-Enabled GPUs\\\\n\\\\nhttps://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus\\\\nlists all CUDA-enabled devices with their compute capability.\\\\nThe compute capability, number of multiprocessors, clock frequency, total amount of device memory, and other properties can be queried using the runtime (see reference manual).\\\\n7.\\\\nC++ Language Extensions\\\\n\\\\n7.1.\\\\nFunction Execution Space Specifiers\\\\n\\\\nFunction execution space specifiers denote whether a function executes on the host or on the device and whether it is callable from the host or from the device.\\\\n7.1.1.\\\\n__global__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__global__\\\\nexecution space specifier declares a function as being a kernel. Such a function is:\\\\nExecuted on the device,\\\\nCallable from the host,\\\\nCallable from the device for devices of compute capability 5.0 or higher (see\\\\nCUDA Dynamic Parallelism\\\\nfor more details).\\\\nA\\\\n__global__\\\\nfunction must have void return type, and cannot be a member of a class.\\\\nAny call to a\\\\n__global__\\\\nfunction must specify its execution configuration as described in\\\\nExecution Configuration\\\\n.\\\\nA call to a\\\\n__global__\\\\nfunction is asynchronous, meaning it returns before the device has completed its execution.\\\\n7.1.2.\\\\n__device__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__device__\\\\nexecution space specifier declares a function that is:\\\\nExecuted on the device,\\\\nCallable from the device only.\\\\nThe\\\\n__global__\\\\nand\\\\n__device__\\\\nexecution space specifiers cannot be used together.\\\\n7.1.3.\\\\n__host__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__host__\\\\nexecution space specifier declares a function that is:\\\\nExecuted on the host,\\\\nCallable from the host only.\\\\nIt is equivalent to declare a function with only the\\\\n__host__\\\\nexecution space specifier or to declare it without any of the\\\\n__host__\\\\n,\\\\n__device__\\\\n, or\\\\n__global__\\\\nexecution space specifier; in either case the function is compiled for the host only.\\\\nThe\\\\n__global__\\\\nand\\\\n__host__\\\\nexecution space specifiers cannot be used together.\\\\nThe\\\\n__device__\\\\nand\\\\n__host__\\\\nexecution space specifiers can be used together however, in which case the function is compiled for both the host and the device. The\\\\n__CUDA_ARCH__\\\\nmacro introduced in\\\\nApplication Compatibility\\\\ncan be used to differentiate code paths between host and device:\\\\n__host__\\\\n__device__\\\\nfunc\\\\n()\\\\n{\\\\n#if __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 800\\\\n// Device code path for compute capability 8.x\\\\n#elif __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 700\\\\n// Device code path for compute capability 7.x\\\\n#elif __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 600\\\\n// Device code path for compute capability 6.x\\\\n#elif __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 500\\\\n// Device code path for compute capability 5.x\\\\n#elif !defined(__CUDA_ARCH__)\\\\n// Host code path\\\\n#endif\\\\n}\\\\n7.1.4.\\\\nUndefined behavior\\\\n\\\\nA ‘cross-execution space’ call has undefined behavior when:\\\\n__CUDA_ARCH__\\\\nis defined, a call from within a\\\\n__global__\\\\n,\\\\n__device__\\\\nor\\\\n__host__\\\\n__device__\\\\nfunction to a\\\\n__host__\\\\nfunction.\\\\n__CUDA_ARCH__\\\\nis undefined, a call from within a\\\\n__host__\\\\nfunction to a\\\\n__device__\\\\nfunction.\\\\n9\\\\n7.1.5.\\\\n__noinline__ and __forceinline__\\\\n\\\\nThe compiler inlines any\\\\n__device__\\\\nfunction when deemed appropriate.\\\\nThe\\\\n__noinline__\\\\nfunction qualifier can be used as a hint for the compiler not to inline the function if possible.\\\\nThe\\\\n__forceinline__\\\\nfunction qualifier can be used to force the compiler to inline the function.\\\\nThe\\\\n__noinline__\\\\nand\\\\n__forceinline__\\\\nfunction qualifiers cannot be used together, and neither function qualifier can be applied to an inline function.\\\\n7.1.6.\\\\n__inline_hint__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__inline_hint__\\\\nqualifier enables more aggressive inlining in the compiler. Unlike\\\\n__forceinline__\\\\n, it does not imply that the function is inline. It can be used to improve inlining across modules when using LTO.\\\\nNeither the\\\\n__noinline__\\\\nnor the\\\\n__forceinline__\\\\nfunction qualifier can be used with the\\\\n__inline_hint__\\\\nfunction qualifier.\\\\n7.2.\\\\nVariable Memory Space Specifiers\\\\n\\\\nVariable memory space specifiers denote the memory location on the device of a variable.\\\\nAn automatic variable declared in device code without any of the\\\\n__device__\\\\n,\\\\n__shared__\\\\nand\\\\n__constant__\\\\nmemory space specifiers described in this section generally resides in a register. However in some cases the compiler might choose to place it in local memory, which can have adverse performance consequences as detailed in\\\\nDevice Memory Accesses\\\\n.\\\\n7.2.1.\\\\n__device__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__device__\\\\nmemory space specifier declares a variable that resides on the device.\\\\nAt most one of the other memory space specifiers defined in the next three sections may be used together with\\\\n__device__\\\\nto further denote which memory space the variable belongs to. If none of them is present, the variable:\\\\nResides in global memory space,\\\\nHas the lifetime of the CUDA context in which it is created,\\\\nHas a distinct object per device,\\\\nIs accessible from all the threads within the grid and from the host through the runtime library\\\\n(cudaGetSymbolAddress()\\\\n/\\\\ncudaGetSymbolSize()\\\\n/\\\\ncudaMemcpyToSymbol()\\\\n/\\\\ncudaMemcpyFromSymbol()\\\\n).\\\\n7.2.2.\\\\n__constant__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__constant__\\\\nmemory space specifier, optionally used together with\\\\n__device__\\\\n, declares a variable that:\\\\nResides in constant memory space,\\\\nHas the lifetime of the CUDA context in which it is created,\\\\nHas a distinct object per device,\\\\nIs accessible from all the threads within the grid and from the host through the runtime library (\\\\ncudaGetSymbolAddress()\\\\n/\\\\ncudaGetSymbolSize()\\\\n/\\\\ncudaMemcpyToSymbol()\\\\n/\\\\ncudaMemcpyFromSymbol()\\\\n).\\\\nThe behavior of modifying a constant from the host while there is a concurrent grid that access that constant at any point of this grid’s lifetime is undefined.\\\\n7.2.3.\\\\n__shared__\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\n__shared__\\\\nmemory space specifier, optionally used together with\\\\n__device__\\\\n, declares a variable that:\\\\nResides in the shared memory space of a thread block,\\\\nHas the lifetime of the block,\\\\nHas a distinct object per block,\\\\nIs only accessible from all the threads within the block,\\\\nDoes not have a constant address.\\\\nWhen declaring a variable in shared memory as an external array such as\\\\nextern\\\\n__shared__\\\\nfloat\\\\nshared\\\\n[];\\\\nthe size of the array is determined at launch time (see\\\\nExecution Configuration\\\\n). All variables declared in this fashion, start at the same address in memory, so that the layout of the variables in the array must be explicitly managed through offsets. For example, if one wants the equivalent of\\\\nshort\\\\narray0\\\\n[\\\\n128\\\\n];\\\\nfloat\\\\narray1\\\\n[\\\\n64\\\\n];\\\\nint\\\\narray2\\\\n[\\\\n256\\\\n];\\\\nin dynamically allocated shared memory, one could declare and initialize the arrays the following way:\\\\nextern\\\\n__shared__\\\\nfloat\\\\narray\\\\n[];\\\\n__de\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 688000:692000]\\\\nCDP2 version of document.\\\\nThe ordering of kernel launches from the device runtime follows CUDA Stream ordering semantics. Within a thread block, all kernel launches into the same stream are executed in-order. With multiple threads in the same thread block launching into the same stream, the ordering within the stream is dependent on the thread scheduling within the block, which may be controlled with synchronization primitives such as\\\\n__syncthreads()\\\\n.\\\\nNote that because streams are shared by all threads within a thread block, the implicit\\\\nNULL\\\\nstream is also shared. If multiple threads in a thread block launch into the implicit stream, then these launches will be executed in-order. If concurrency is desired, explicit named streams should be used.\\\\nDynamic Parallelism\\\\nenables concurrency to be expressed more easily within a program; however, the device runtime introduces no new concurrency guarantees within the CUDA execution model. There is no guarantee of concurrent execution between any number of different thread blocks on a device.\\\\nThe lack of concurrency guarantee extends to parent thread blocks and their child grids. When a parent thread block launches a child grid, the child is not guaranteed to begin execution until the parent thread block reaches an explicit synchronization point (such as\\\\ncudaDeviceSynchronize()\\\\n).\\\\nWarning\\\\nExplicit synchronization with child kernels from a parent block (i.e. using\\\\ncudaDeviceSynchronize()\\\\nin device code) is deprecated in CUDA 11.6, removed for compute_90+ compilation, and is slated for full removal in a future CUDA release.\\\\nWhile concurrency will often easily be achieved, it may vary as a function of deviceconfiguration, application workload, and runtime scheduling. It is therefore unsafe to depend upon any concurrency between different thread blocks.\\\\n9.6.1.1.6.\\\\nDevice Management (CDP1)\\\\n\\\\nSee\\\\nDevice Management\\\\n, above, for CDP2 version of document.\\\\nThere is no multi-GPU support from the device runtime; the device runtime is only capable of operating on the device upon which it is currently executing. It is permitted, however, to query properties for any CUDA capable device in the system.\\\\n9.6.1.2.\\\\nMemory Model (CDP1)\\\\n\\\\nSee\\\\nMemory Model\\\\n, above, for CDP2 version of document.\\\\nParent and child grids share the same global and constant memory storage, but have distinct local and shared memory.\\\\n9.6.1.2.1.\\\\nCoherence and Consistency (CDP1)\\\\n\\\\nSee\\\\nCoherence and Consistency\\\\n, above, for CDP2 version of document.\\\\n9.6.1.2.1.1.\\\\nGlobal Memory (CDP1)\\\\n\\\\nSee\\\\nGlobal Memory\\\\n, above, for CDP2 version of document.\\\\nParent and child grids have coherent access to global memory, with weak consistency guarantees between child and parent. There are two points in the execution of a child grid when its view of memory is fully consistent with the parent thread: when the child grid is invoked by the parent, and when the child grid completes as signaled by a synchronization API invocation in the parent thread.\\\\nWarning\\\\nExplicit synchronization with child kernels from a parent block (i.e. using\\\\ncudaDeviceSynchronize()\\\\nin device code) is deprecated in CUDA 11.6, removed for compute_90+ compilation, and is slated for full removal in a future CUDA release.\\\\nAll global memory operations in the parent thread prior to the child grid’s invocation are visible to the child grid. All memory operations of the child grid are visible to the parent after the parent has synchronized on the child grid’s completion.\\\\nIn the following example, the child grid executing\\\\nchild_launch\\\\nis only guaranteed to see the modifications to\\\\ndata\\\\nmade before the child grid was launched. Since thread 0 of the parent is performing the launch, the child will be consistent with the memory seen by thread 0 of the parent. Due to the first\\\\n__syncthreads()\\\\ncall, the child will see\\\\ndata[0]=0\\\\n,\\\\ndata[1]=1\\\\n, …,\\\\ndata[255]=255\\\\n(without the\\\\n__syncthreads()\\\\ncall, only\\\\ndata[0]\\\\nwould be guaranteed to be seen by the child). When the child grid returns, thread 0 is guaranteed \\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 948000:956000]\\\\nre cache and L2 or in L2 only) can be partially configured on a per-access basis using modifiers to the load instruction.\\\\n16.5.2.\\\\nGlobal Memory\\\\n\\\\nGlobal memory behaves the same way as in devices of compute capability 5.x (See\\\\nGlobal Memory\\\\n).\\\\n16.5.3.\\\\nShared Memory\\\\n\\\\nShared memory behaves the same way as in devices of compute capability 5.x (See\\\\nShared Memory\\\\n).\\\\n16.6.\\\\nCompute Capability 7.x\\\\n\\\\n16.6.1.\\\\nArchitecture\\\\n\\\\nAn SM consists of:\\\\n64 FP32 cores for single-precision arithmetic operations,\\\\n32 FP64 cores for double-precision arithmetic operations,\\\\n34\\\\n64 INT32 cores for integer math,\\\\n8 mixed-precision Tensor Cores for deep learning matrix arithmetic\\\\n16 special function units for single-precision floating-point transcendental functions,\\\\n4 warp schedulers.\\\\nAn SM statically distributes its warps among its schedulers. Then, at every instruction issue time, each scheduler issues one instruction for one of its assigned warps that is ready to execute, if any.\\\\nAn SM has:\\\\na read-only constant cache that is shared by all functional units and speeds up reads from the constant memory space, which resides in device memory,\\\\na unified data cache and shared memory with a total size of 128 KB (\\\\nVolta\\\\n) or 96 KB (\\\\nTuring\\\\n).\\\\nShared memory is partitioned out of unified data cache, and can be configured to various sizes (See\\\\nShared Memory\\\\n.) The remaining data cache serves as an L1 cache and is also used by the texture unit that implements the various addressing and data filtering modes mentioned in\\\\nTexture and Surface Memory\\\\n.\\\\n16.6.2.\\\\nIndependent Thread Scheduling\\\\n\\\\nThe\\\\nVolta\\\\narchitecture introduces\\\\nIndependent Thread Scheduling\\\\namong threads in a warp, enabling intra-warp synchronization patterns previously unavailable and simplifying code changes when porting CPU code. However, this can lead to a rather different set of threads participating in the executed code than intended if the developer made assumptions about warp-synchronicity of previous hardware architectures.\\\\nBelow are code patterns of concern and suggested corrective actions for Volta-safe code.\\\\nFor applications using warp intrinsics (\\\\n__shfl*\\\\n,\\\\n__any\\\\n,\\\\n__all\\\\n,\\\\n__ballot\\\\n), it is necessary that developers port their code to the new, safe, synchronizing counterpart, with the\\\\n*_sync\\\\nsuffix. The new warp intrinsics take in a mask of threads that explicitly define which lanes (threads of a warp) must participate in the warp intrinsic. See\\\\nWarp Vote Functions\\\\nand\\\\nWarp Shuffle Functions\\\\nfor details.\\\\nSince the intrinsics are available with CUDA 9.0+, (if necessary) code can be executed conditionally with the following preprocessor macro:\\\\n#if defined(CUDART_VERSION) && CUDART_VERSION >= 9000\\\\n// *_sync intrinsic\\\\n#endif\\\\nThese intrinsics are available on all architectures, not just\\\\nVolta\\\\nor\\\\nTuring\\\\n, and in most cases a single code-base will suffice for all architectures. Note, however, that for\\\\nPascal\\\\nand earlier architectures, all threads in mask must execute the same warp intrinsic instruction in convergence, and the union of all values in mask must be equal to the warp’s active mask. The following code pattern is valid on\\\\nVolta\\\\n, but not on\\\\nPascal\\\\nor earlier architectures.\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\ntid\\\\n%\\\\nwarpSize\\\\n<\\\\n16\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\n...\\\\nfloat\\\\nswapped\\\\n=\\\\n__shfl_xor_sync\\\\n(\\\\n0xffffffff\\\\n,\\\\nval\\\\n,\\\\n16\\\\n);\\\\n...\\\\n}\\\\nelse\\\\n{\\\\n...\\\\nfloat\\\\nswapped\\\\n=\\\\n__shfl_xor_sync\\\\n(\\\\n0xffffffff\\\\n,\\\\nval\\\\n,\\\\n16\\\\n);\\\\n...\\\\n}\\\\nThe replacement for\\\\n__ballot(1)\\\\nis\\\\n__activemask()\\\\n. Note that threads within a warp can diverge even within a single code path. As a result,\\\\n__activemask()\\\\nand\\\\n__ballot(1)\\\\nmay return only a subset of the threads on the current code path. The following invalid code example sets bit\\\\ni\\\\nof\\\\noutput\\\\nto 1 when\\\\ndata[i]\\\\nis greater than\\\\nthreshold\\\\n.\\\\n__activemask()\\\\nis used in an attempt to enable cases where\\\\ndataLen\\\\nis not a multiple of 32.\\\\n// Sets bit in output[] to 1 if the correspond element in data[i]\\\\n// is greater than 'threshold', using 32 threads in a warp.\\\\nfor\\\\n(\\\\nint\\\\ni\\\\n=\\\\nwarpLane\\\\n;\\\\ni\\\\n<\\\\ndataLen\\\\n;\\\\ni\\\\n+=\\\\nwarpSize\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\nunsigned\\\\nactive\\\\n=\\\\n__activemask\\\\n();\\\\nunsigned\\\\nbitPack\\\\n=\\\\n__ballot_sync\\\\n(\\\\nactive\\\\n,\\\\ndata\\\\n[\\\\ni\\\\n]\\\\n>\\\\nthreshold\\\\n);\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\nwarpLane\\\\n==\\\\n0\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\noutput\\\\n[\\\\ni\\\\n/\\\\n32\\\\n]\\\\n=\\\\nbitPack\\\\n;\\\\n}\\\\n}\\\\nThis code is invalid because CUDA does not guarantee that the warp will diverge ONLY at the loop condition. When divergence happens for other reasons, conflicting results will be computed for the same 32-bit output element by different subsets of threads in the warp. A correct code might use a non-divergent loop condition together with\\\\n__ballot_sync()\\\\nto safely enumerate the set of threads in the warp participating in the threshold calculation as follows.\\\\nfor\\\\n(\\\\nint\\\\ni\\\\n=\\\\nwarpLane\\\\n;\\\\ni\\\\n-\\\\nwarpLane\\\\n<\\\\ndataLen\\\\n;\\\\ni\\\\n+=\\\\nwarpSize\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\nunsigned\\\\nactive\\\\n=\\\\n__ballot_sync\\\\n(\\\\n0xFFFFFFFF\\\\n,\\\\ni\\\\n<\\\\ndataLen\\\\n);\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\ni\\\\n<\\\\ndataLen\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\nunsigned\\\\nbitPack\\\\n=\\\\n__ballot_sync\\\\n(\\\\nactive\\\\n,\\\\ndata\\\\n[\\\\ni\\\\n]\\\\n>\\\\nthreshold\\\\n);\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\nwarpLane\\\\n==\\\\n0\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\noutput\\\\n[\\\\ni\\\\n/\\\\n32\\\\n]\\\\n=\\\\nbitPack\\\\n;\\\\n}\\\\n}\\\\n}\\\\nDiscovery Pattern\\\\ndemonstrates a valid use case for\\\\n__activemask()\\\\n.\\\\nIf applications have warp-synchronous codes, they will need to insert the new\\\\n__syncwarp()\\\\nwarp-wide barrier synchronization instruction between any steps where data is exchanged between threads via global or shared memory. Assumptions that code is executed in lockstep or that reads/writes from separate threads are visible across a warp without synchronization are invalid.\\\\n__shared__\\\\nfloat\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\nBLOCK_SIZE\\\\n];\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n]\\\\n=\\\\nval\\\\n;\\\\n__syncthreads\\\\n();\\\\n// Inter-warp reduction\\\\nfor\\\\n(\\\\nint\\\\ni\\\\n=\\\\nBLOCK_SIZE\\\\n/\\\\n2\\\\n;\\\\ni\\\\n>=\\\\n32\\\\n;\\\\ni\\\\n/=\\\\n2\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\ntid\\\\n<\\\\ni\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n]\\\\n+=\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n+\\\\ni\\\\n];\\\\n}\\\\n__syncthreads\\\\n();\\\\n}\\\\n// Intra-warp reduction\\\\n// Butterfly reduction simplifies syncwarp mask\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\ntid\\\\n<\\\\n32\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\nfloat\\\\ntemp\\\\n;\\\\ntemp\\\\n=\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n^\\\\n16\\\\n];\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n]\\\\n+=\\\\ntemp\\\\n;\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ntemp\\\\n=\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n^\\\\n8\\\\n];\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n]\\\\n+=\\\\ntemp\\\\n;\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ntemp\\\\n=\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n^\\\\n4\\\\n];\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n]\\\\n+=\\\\ntemp\\\\n;\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ntemp\\\\n=\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n^\\\\n2\\\\n];\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\ntid\\\\n]\\\\n+=\\\\ntemp\\\\n;\\\\n__syncwarp\\\\n();\\\\n}\\\\nif\\\\n(\\\\ntid\\\\n==\\\\n0\\\\n)\\\\n{\\\\n*\\\\noutput\\\\n=\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\n0\\\\n]\\\\n+\\\\ns_buff\\\\n[\\\\n1\\\\n];\\\\n}\\\\n__syncthreads\\\\n();\\\\nAlthough\\\\n__syncthreads()\\\\nhas been consistently documented as synchronizing all threads in the thread block,\\\\nPascal\\\\nand prior architectures could only enforce synchronization at the warp level. In certain cases, this allowed a barrier to succeed without being executed by every thread as long as at least some thread in every warp reached the barrier. Starting with\\\\nVolta\\\\n, the CUDA built-in\\\\n__syncthreads()\\\\nand PTX instruction\\\\nbar.sync\\\\n(and their derivatives) are enforced per thread and thus will not succeed until reached by all non-exited threads in the block. Code exploiting the previous behavior will likely deadlock and must be modified to ensure that all non-exited threads reach the barrier.\\\\nThe\\\\nracecheck\\\\nand\\\\nsynccheck\\\\ntools provided by\\\\ncompute-saniter\\\\ncan help with locating violations.\\\\nTo aid migration while implementing the above-mentioned corrective actions, developers can opt-in to the Pascal scheduling model that does not support independent thread scheduling. For the\\\\nVolta\\\\narchitecture (compute capability 7.0), the unified data cache has a size of 128 KB, and the shared memory capacity can be set to 0, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 96 KB. For the\\\\nTuring\\\\narchitecture (compute capability 7.5), the unified data cache has a size of 96 KB, and the shared memory capacity can be set to either 32 KB or 64 KB. Unlike Kepler, the driver automatically configures the shared memory capacity for each kernel to avoid shared memory occupancy bottlenecks while also allowing concurrent execution with already launched kernels where possible. In most cases, the driver’s default behavior should provide optimal performance.\\\\nBecause the driver is not always aware of\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 1024000:1028000]\\\\nity.\\\\nThere are two main ways to obtain CUDA Unified Memory:\\\\nSystem-Allocated Memory\\\\n: memory allocated on the host with system APIs:\\\\n\\\\nstack variables, global-/file-scope variables,\\\\nmalloc()\\\\n/\\\\nmmap()\\\\n(see\\\\nSystem-Allocated Memory: in-depth examples\\\\nfor in-depth examples), thread locals, etc.\\\\nCUDA APIs that explicitly allocate Unified Memory\\\\n: memory allocated with, for example,\\\\ncudaMallocManaged()\\\\n,\\\\n\\\\nare available on more systems and may perform better than System-Allocated Memory.\\\\n19.1.1.\\\\nSystem Requirements for Unified Memory\\\\n\\\\nThe following table shows the different levels of support for CUDA Unified Memory,\\\\n\\\\nthe device properties required to detect these levels of support\\\\n\\\\nand links to the documentation specific to each level of support:\\\\nTable 28\\\\nOverview of levels of unified memory support\\\\n\\\\nUnified Memory Support Level\\\\nSystem device properties\\\\nFurther documentation\\\\nFull CUDA Unified Memory: all memory has full support.
